story_text.value:
Balk is a baseball game. Things like MLB Showdown and other baseball games captured my attention growing up, but never really filled the void of a game. They were fun to look at and scheme, but the game itself was missing something. I think baseball lends itself really well to game design. There are a lot of games that exist inside the game of baseball. It’s a deeply flawed and broken sport, but so are humans, and in some ways that makes baseball better.

It’s baseball. You already know the rules, and that’s the point. You play against another person, or against Tin Pete, the bot. A game takes about 30 minutes, honestly I’m not sure, I can play it fast but I’m using the hotkeys.

It’s what I’d consider alpha, and I’m still trying to find what’s fun. It’s been a nice outlet and a break from solving business problems, though the same skill set gets invoked: distill a complex idea down to its most basic implementation.

Stack is Java, React, Postgres, on a $5 Digital Ocean instance. I'm sure you can bring it down if you are bored.

There’s some slop TOS and privacy policy up. No trackers, nothing sold. Happy to update the intention was that these were easy to understand and I'm not interested in selling your data.

If you want to see how it was built, day by day, counted from the repo: https://balk.club/blog/timeline.html

story_text.value:
A lot of people love hacker news because the website is simple, fast, and its UI stays out of the way.

I just can't seem to leave well enough alone

I built HackerFlow because I wanted to browse HN visually while keeping articles and comments in the same place.The goal is a fast UI that stays out of the way but offers more visuals. I tried a few other GUIs and none of them really satisfied me.

Features:

- Gallery, magazine, list and compact views - Inline article reader with rendered text and page previews - Infinite scrolling with thumbnail preloading - Collapsible comments, capped indentation and next-parent navigation - Preserved scroll position when opening stories or navigating back - Search, local bookmarks, dark mode and keyboard shortcuts - Responsive layouts and an installable web app - Bookmarked articles stored in your browser

no monetization, no accounts.

story_text.value:
In this demo, we automatically deduce a FlashAttention kernel with ~25 lines of SQL, which just expresses vanilla attention. This is possible due to three portable SQL extensions that we’re building: - xarray-sql: a library that efficiently represents petabyte scale array datasets in the cloud as tables (relations). - ddx: a database extension that adds automatic differentiation in the style of JAX to standard SQL, assuming the above array data model. - einfold: a modular query planner for fast tensor contractions in vanilla SQL, again, assuming the above array data model.

My hope is that the relational model and algebra provide fresh perspectives on how we might do accelerator programming. Here, our thesis is that separating the logical layers in a tensor program from the physical layers is both more correct and more scalable.

If the Bitter Lesson is a central dogma of machine learning, then why not formalize it with relational algebra?

If this interests you and you’d like to tinker with us at the intersection of database theory and ML systems, join us on Discord at https://xql.systems (link at the bottom). Cheers.

story_text.value:
Hello my beloved tech forum!

Earlier this year I moved to a new apartment, and scattered a box of poetry magnets all over my fridge. Whenever people came to visit, I noticed how they always loved making poems of their own, not to mention enjoying the poems others had already created. It became such a fun and entertaining tradition, (especially due to the range of creative messages that my friends chose) that I felt compelled to make a full stack project out of it.

While LLM agents have made the technical aspects of building a project like this easier, it took me a really long time to nail the algorithm for choosing daily word sets. I started with a huge collection (on the order of 100,000) of words, grouped by part of speech and sorted by the frequency of use in English. I tried randomly choosing a few words in the top 10, a few in the top 100, and so on, for each part of speech.

That straight up did not work. Trying to make poetry out of those wordsets felt terrible. It was very discouraging. I had to go back to the drawing board many times. My current solution came about when I found some databases of words, one sorted by their sensory value (from most to least sensory-evoking) and one where words are sorted on a spectrum of concreteness to abstractness.

Another key to picking fun and interesting word sets was ensuring there are a solid set of words that are included in every set no matter what. This "glue" set was handpicked by words that I found myself searching for over and over again when trying to write poems, but it is deliberately small to help people be creative in how they express ideas.

I used Deepseek v4.1 Flash and the Pi agent. My AGENTS.md emphasizes my status as a junior developer, specifically prompting the agent to never make architectural decisions on my behalf, to quiz me on the architecture/code involved before implementing changes I request, and to never write copy so I can make sure the site feels warm and genuine in my own words. I wanted to avoid letting the code get out of control for when I want to add features in the future.

One of the things I love about building these kinds of projects that LLMs enable is being able to add tiny features that most people will never see. For example, I added special effects that occur when a haiku is written.

I chose TanStack Start and React this time instead of SvelteKit. The experience was about the same. And kudos on poems are deliberately spammable. I like seeing number go up.

Friends have expressed enjoyment from using it so far, but I'm excited to hear feedback on y'all's experience and see if there's anything huge I'm missing. Thank you in advance!

title.value: Show HN: A Daily Poem Writing Puzzle

story_text.value:
Hey Everyone,

At work, and for several of our employees at home too, we've been big users of shared storage. We have a big TrueNAS storage server at the office containing a mix of spinning rust and flash. In addition to SMB and NFS, we've been big users of iSCSI for our Linux and Windows servers and clients.

But all of our employees use Macs, and due to the lack of modern iSCSI initiator software for Mac we were never able to utilize iSCSI for Mac clients. Existing legacy iSCSI initiators for Mac use kernel extensions that require turning off System Integrity Protection in recovery mode to install on Apple Silicon Macs.

That's insane. You shouldn't have to severely sacrifice your Mac's security to use iSCSI! So, we built a high performance user-mode iSCSI initiator for macOS. Our solution is a sandboxed Mac App Store application that requires no Kernel Extensions, no drivers, no reduced security and no reboots to install.

Introducing BeamDisk, the first high-performance user-mode iSCSI initiator for macOS without security compromises.

BeamDisk allows you to mount LUNs from your storage server, NAS, or Enterprise SAN arrays directly to your Mac and have them show up as standard disks. You can format the LUNs APFS, HFS+, any format you like.

BeamDisk can easily saturate a 10 Gigabit Ethernet connection and hits tens of thousands of random R/W IOPs on standard SATA SSDs. All of the benchmarks on our site were recorded on our own hardware on an M4 Mac Mini over 10 GbE with no special tricks.

Even just standard Time Machine backups to APFS LUNs are far more performant and MUCH more reliable than Time Machine over SMB.

Today, we're releasing our first public beta via Apple's TestFlight. Beta spots are currently limited to 100, first come first served. Beta users will have access to all features, for free, forever.

Once we land in the Mac App Store, BeamDisk will have a 30-day trial with all features unlocked and then will be free for basic Home users and paid ($25) for business use.

For you prosumers out there with massive homelabs (our kind of people) the free version's limits can be lifted via an in-app purchase once BeamDisk is on the App Store. For TestFlight testers everything is unlocked, forever.

Happy to answer any questions you have and collect feedback to share with the team. Otherwise, give it a shot and get your LUNs "Beamed" to your Mac!

BeamDisk.app - https://BeamDisk.app

Community GitHub Repo for Discussions, Issues, Roadmap, etc - https://github.com/3rdBitLabs/BeamDisk

Have a great weekend!

title.value: Show HN: BeamDisk – High Performance iSCSI Initiator for macOS

story_text.value:
I have built a cosy fish tank simulation you can leave on a large screen and watch from time to time. I like pixel art but didn’t want to be religious about it, so I think of it as pixel art adjacent.

This summer, down with the flu, I started a small experiment. It ended up taking about 50-70 hours of my time, iterating over several months.

There is a 24-inch display in my kitchen powered by a used Lenovo mini PC (previously it was a RPi, but I had to upgrade to get a better GPU). I used it to show a rotation of my home photos, but now I’ve switched it to show this fish tank.

No prior game dev experience, but years of backend development and all the time spent reading indie dev blogs (honourable mentions Factorio and Banished) helped.

I used LLMs to give me a hand. It rather felt like playing a game, maybe like Factorio a bit, switching from system design to art direction and back and learning more about game dev to make it look better and better. For me it became a way to express creativity I might otherwise not have had time for. Along the way I learned what marine snow is and how fish swim. One funny story was me curiously asking an LLM if it could find some research papers on fish swimming patterns and styles and base the implementation on that, and it did.

I also used it to create a surprise for my wife’s birthday: on the day, three fish with QR codes appeared, each leading to a quest in the real world. But that is another story. Halloween is around the corner, so try the Halloween theme.

title.value: Show HN: Fishoid: an ambient fish tank for your screen

story_text.value:
Hi HN,

I built Pollsight, an simple civic web application that aims to solve the problem of the amount of time++research needed to vote based on your preferences on an overwhelming amount of races and referendums by collecting data from various sources and aggregating and summarizing that content in line with what you care about.

In Austin we have 53 Races, and 10 Propositions to vote on, and never enough time to devote to understand what each issue and candidate is about. So I built something to help with this process.

What it does is collects info from a number of different places: social media, candidate websites, OpenFEC, Vote411, and other places, and utilizes that using a RAG db + your preferred interests + AI to rank candidates most inline with your interests and with summaries (with sources) of the "why".

Would love feedback, especially on certain regions that don't have enough data (it's surprisingly hard to find everything!).

Hope this helps! Now get out there and vote!

title.value: Show HN: Pollsight – a simple tool to aid ballot research
